mix.summary_plain:
1. The 80 billion pieces come from about 30 public datasets. Roughly 40% is good educational web pages, 9% textbook-style writing, 12% code (Python first) and 6% explanations of computers (Stack Overflow-style answers, manuals, open textbooks, and web pages picked out by their topic labels). The rest is about 9.5% maths, 7% Wikipedia, 5% books, 5% questions and answers, 3% science papers and 3% chats.
2. There is far more good text than we need, so almost every source is read once or less. Only small, very good sources (Simple Wikipedia, manuals, small maths sets, some chats) are read 2 to 4 times, and nothing more than 4.
3. The run has three parts. The first 70 billion pieces are read in windows of 4,096. The next 8 billion use only the best parts (top-rated pages, the best code, worked maths, more chat), as the pico's last stretch did. The last 2 billion use windows of 16,384: mostly whole books, papers and code projects, mixed with some of the best short text.
4. Before training, the text is cleaned on a cheap separate computer. Copies and near-copies are removed, along with non-English text and junk. Any text containing the questions from your own tests or from the standard public tests is also removed, so the scores stay honest.
5. Compared with the draft, textbook-style writing drops from 15% to 9% and chats from 5% to 3%. Both are written by other AI models and can carry made-up facts, and published small models used less of them. The freed room goes to a second kind of web text that reads more like people explaining things.
6. The download is about 450 GB, and preparing it takes roughly 8 to 13 hours on a 32-core computer, so no GPU time is spent waiting.
7. A few things need your decision: the licence points, whether to use the optional NVIDIA question set, and how chats should be laid out (which special markers). The chats also teach behaviour, so their filters need your yes: no other AI's name and no canned refusals.

mix.anneal_phase:
Pieces 70-78B (8B, 10%), window 4,096, while the learning rate falls (the decay continues through the long phase to 80B). Same sources, best slices only. This mirrors the pico's last stretch, which dropped its lower-rated FineWeb and raised the best material.

Shares of the 8B:
- **Web 25%:** FineWeb-Edu int_score >= 4 17%, DCLM-Edu edu_int_score >= 4 8%.
- **Cosmopedia 5%:** college/textbook formats, CS/maths/science topics.
- **Nemotron Diverse QA 2%.**
- **Code 18%:** Stack-Edu Python int_score >= 4 7%, other languages >= 4 6%, Kaggle notebooks 1.5%, OpenCoder annealing Q&A and snippets 3.5%.
- **CS knowledge 8%:** Stack Exchange tech answers with pm_score >= 4 or accepted 4%, Essential-Web CS pages at undergraduate level or above 2%, docs and open textbooks 1%, FinePDFs-Edu CS 1%.
- **Maths 15%:** FineMath-4+ 7%, Math SE top answers 2%, worked problems 6% (Orca-Math, MetaMathQA, OpenMathInstruct-2 1M, NuminaMath school level, TinyGSM, GSM8K train).
- **Wikipedia 9%:** FineWiki 7.5%, Simple 1.5%.
- **Books 3%:** DOAB 2%, Gutenberg 1%.
- **Non-tech Stack Exchange top answers 3%.**
- **Science 2%:** arXiv abstracts 1%, peS2o 1%.
- **Conversation 10%:** SmolTalk 5%, WildChat English 2%, UltraChat 1.5%, SODA 1.5%, in the fine-tune's exact layout.

Why these changes:
- Code rises from 11% to 18% and maths from 9% to 15%, as in the SmolLM2/SmolLM3 decays (code 24%, maths 13-14%). Both kept their best maths and code for the decay.
- Chat rises from 2.5% to 10%. This follows MiniCPM, where SFT-style data in the decay gave MMLU 44.6 -> 50.9 and GSM8K 27.7 -> 42.3 at 2.4B. It stays below the pico's ~25% because published small models used 0-2%.

The same mix is also:
- the pool for the fine-tune's 8% plain-text replay (text the model already knows);
- the 40% short part of the long phase.

Save checkpoints at 70B (before the anneal) and at 74B so the owner can compare.
mix.long_phase:
Pieces 78-80B (2B, 2.5%), window 16,384, with the learning rate still falling.

Settings:
- Raise the rotary base at the switch to about 1,000,000 (Qwen-style ABF; Men et al. 2024 give ~3.1e5 as the minimum for 16K).
- Mask attention at document boundaries.

Long documents, 60% (1.2B). Each is 8k-16k+ pieces, one per window where possible; books are cut at paragraph breaks.
- **Books 25%:** Gutenberg 15% (without PG-19's test and validation books), DOAB 10% (only documents long enough).
- **Papers 15%:** Common Pile arXiv full papers 10%, peS2o 5% (cs, math, physics first).
- **Code repositories 12%:** Stack-Edu files of one repo joined with file-name headers, Python first.
- **Long articles and CS textbooks 8%:** FinePDFs-Edu long documents 5%, long FineWiki articles 2%, open textbooks (OpenStax Intro CS, LibreTexts CS, full Python docs pages) 1%.

Short text, 40% (0.8B): the anneal mix in its own shares, packed with document masking.

Evidence:
- ProLong: about 60% long / 40% short was best; code repositories and books were the best long data; 100% long hurt both long and short skill; masking across documents helped.
- Fu et al. 2024: 0.5-5B tokens are enough, and the domain balance should be kept.
- SmolLM3: more long data than this gave no extra RULER/HELMET gain.

Supply is far above need (Gutenberg alone is ~5B pieces).

Checks:
- wrongness by position on the held-out PG-19 test books (not perplexity alone, which ProLong found misleading);
- a needle-in-a-haystack test at 4k, 8k and 16k;
- the normal short tests (held-out text, 117-question quiz, sums, chat_suite), which must not drop.
mix.cleaning:
All on the separate CPU machine, in this order. Each step runs first on ~500 documents per source with samples read (pico lesson), then on everything.

**1. Format**
- One plain-text document per item: UTF-8, NFC, newlines kept.
- Stack Exchange HTML becomes text, with code blocks fenced and lists kept.
- Chats are rewritten into the fine-tune's exact layout, with an end-of-turn mark after every assistant turn.

**2. Language**
- fastText lid.176 English >= 0.65 on prose sources not already English-filtered: Stack Exchange, DOAB, peS2o, arXiv, WildChat, LibreTexts/PressBooks, ArchWiki (lang=en).
- Markdown >= 0.5; code files are not language-checked.

**3. Quality and boilerplate**
- Prose: drop documents under 50 words. On web, PDFs and books, apply Gopher-style repetition rules (duplicate lines > 30%, top 2-gram > 20%) and drop lines repeated across many documents of a shard (menus, cookie notices, 'share this').
- PDFs: remove running headers and page numbers, join hyphenated line breaks, drop documents under 70% letters or with broken extraction.
- Gutenberg: drop transcriber notes, contents pages and index pages.
- Stack Exchange: keep the accepted answer plus at most 2 more with pm_score >= 2. Drop answers under 20 words and 'possible duplicate' / 'what have you tried' replies, and drop questions with no answer left.
- Code:
  - Drop generated and vendor files (metadata flags), files over 100 KB, minified files (average line > 100 characters or any line > 1,000), mostly-data files (letters < 25%) and base64/hex blobs.
  - Replace secrets, keys, emails and IP addresses with placeholders.
- Conversation (behaviour filters; the owner approves these before building, per the 'ask before behaviour choices' rule):
  - Drop non-English chats and WildChat's toxic-flagged ones.
  - Drop chats where the assistant calls itself another assistant or company (SmolLM, ChatGPT, GPT-4, OpenAI, Claude, Llama, Qwen, Gemma, 'As an AI language model').
  - Drop assistant turns that are only a canned refusal or only 'I don't know', drop knowledge-cutoff claims and drop function-calling items.
  - No passage-reading practice and no 'The text doesn't say.' anywhere in pretraining.

**4. Exact duplicates**
- SHA-256 of the lower-cased, whitespace-collapsed text across all sources. Keep the first copy, in this priority order: FineWiki, books, Stack Exchange, FineWeb-Edu, DCLM-Edu, Essential-Web, others.
- URL duplicates: drop DCLM-Edu and Essential-Web pages whose URL is in the FineWeb-Edu sample.

**5. Near duplicates**
- MinHash LSH (5-word shingles, 112 hashes in 14 bands of 8, about 0.8 similarity) over all real prose as one pool: web rows, Essential-Web, FinePDFs, Stack Exchange, FineWiki, books, papers. This also removes Wikipedia mirrors from the web sets.
- Not run between FineMath and InfiWebMath (HF found that hurt), and not over code (already deduplicated in The Stack v2) or the small synthetic sets.

**6. Held-out text**
- 1 document in 100 per source is set aside by a fixed hash of its id before training. It is never trained on, and the same list is used for every 560M run.
- The pico's own held-out documents (decoded from data/slinger/*/val.bin) are also removed, so per-letter wrongness can be compared fairly between the pico and the 560M.
- Kept out as well: PG-19 test/validation books, the SmolTalk and UltraChat test splits, GSM8K test.

**7. Decontamination against the project's own tests**
The lists are imported at build time, so later tests must be added before building:
- research/test_slinger.py: CHAT 12, LOOKUP_QUESTIONS 30, BROAD_QUESTIONS 30, IDENTITY_QUESTIONS 10, NONSENSE_QUESTIONS 10.
- research/chat_suite.py: FACTS 30 casual + 30 formal, SUMS 10, the SWITCH/WRONG/FOLLOW chats and their questions, LONG 8, GREET 6, WHO 4, INSTRUCT 4, IMPOSSIBLE 10, LATE 4.
- research/facts_quiz.py QUIZ.
- finetune_slinger.arithmetic_test(): 50 sums, seed 2026.

Rules:
- In every source, drop documents that contain a test question verbatim (after lower-casing and stripping punctuation) or one of chat_suite's prepared assistant replies.
- In question-shaped sources (chats, Stack Exchange, Nemotron QA, worked problems), also drop items whose question has >= 80% of a test question's content words and is at most 1.5x as long, and exact copies of the 50 sums.
- Deliberately not done as topic removal. The fine-tune's test_words title rule (drop any article whose title shares a test word) would remove Paris, Japan, photosynthesis and the other facts the quiz checks the model learned from ordinary text, so that rule stays in the fine-tune only.

**8. Decontamination against public tests**
- Tests covered: MMLU (all splits), HellaSwag (val+test), ARC Easy/Challenge, GSM8K and MATH test, PIQA, OpenBookQA, CommonsenseQA, WinoGrande, HumanEval (164) and MBPP (974).
- Prose: word 13-grams of question + choices + answer, lower-cased and without punctuation. A document sharing one is dropped; for books, papers and other long documents only the paragraph is dropped. Items under 13 words are matched as whole normalised strings.
- Code: drop files containing a HumanEval/MBPP prompt or docstring (whitespace-normalised) or a 13-token run of a canonical solution, and repositories named after the benchmarks.
- Output: a count of removals per source and per test. It is a report only; the owner decides on anything unexpected.
mix.tokenizer:
A 16,384-piece byte-level BPE, built with HF tokenizers like the pico's prepare_slinger.py (ByteLevel with the full 256-byte starting alphabet). It is trained on a ~3 GB sample (about 750M pieces) of the cleaned and decontaminated text, with each document capped at 20 KB so no single book dominates.

Sample shares:
- **Web 35%:** FineWeb-Edu 21, DCLM-Edu 14.
- **Cosmopedia 7%.**
- **Code 20%:** Python 8, JS/TS 3, C/C++ 2.5, Java+C# 2, SQL+Shell 1.5, Go/Rust/PHP/Ruby/Swift 1.5, HTML+Markdown 1.5.
- **CS prose 8%:** Stack Exchange tech, docs, Essential-Web CS.
- **Maths 10%:** FineMath with LaTeX, Math SE, worked problems.
- **Wikipedia 8%, books 4%, science 3%.**
- **Conversation 5%,** in the exact chat layout.

Code and maths sit above their training shares so that indentation runs, keywords (def, return, self.) and LaTeX commands get their own pieces.

Pre-tokenizer:
- pre_tokenizers.Sequence([Digits(individual_digits=True), ByteLevel(add_prefix_space=False)]). Every digit is its own piece, so numbers are read digit by digit, which helps sums. The GPT-2-style split keeps runs of spaces and tabs as indentation pieces.
- No Unicode normalisation inside the tokenizer, so code stays exact (NFC is done in cleaning).

Special pieces: reserve 16.
- End-of-text as id 0, as in the pico.
- System, user and assistant turn markers and an end-of-turn marker.
- Search-call and search-result markers.
- Spares.
Whether the chat layout switches from the pico's 'User:/Assistant:' text lines to these markers is the owner's decision. It must be made before the chat data is written, because pretraining chats and the fine-tune must match.

Checks after training:
- Letters per piece per source on held-out text: about 4 on prose, about 3-3.5 on code.
- Exact round-trip decode on 10,000 documents.
- Per-source piece counts, which replace every estimate in the table before shares and passes are fixed.

Training takes roughly 20-40 minutes on the CPU machine (about 64 GB of RAM).
lessons_applied: Keep test questions' words out of practice data (test_words). In pretraining this becomes exact and near-exact question matching in every source and in question-shaped sources, not topic removal. The 117-question quiz checks facts the model should learn from ordinary text, so the title rule stays in the fine-tune. The test lists are imported from test_slinger.py, chat_suite.py and facts_quiz.py at build time.

Approving a dataset is not approving the behaviour it teaches. Chats in pretraining teach behaviour, so the conversation filters go to the owner for a yes before the data is built: other assistants' names removed, canned refusals and 'As an AI language model' removed, no 'I don't know' practice, no 'The text doesn't say.'.

SQuAD 2.0's unanswerable third leaked 'The text doesn't say.' into 165 of 1,300 chats and taught narrow answers. So there is no SQuAD or other passage-reading practice in pretraining; reading practice stays in the fine-tune, answerable questions only.

Never feed the model's own answers back as training text. Nothing written by SlingerGPT is in the mix. Text written by other models is capped at about 16-17% (Cosmopedia, Nemotron, worked problems, OpenCoder, chat replies), so real text stays above 80%.

Fine-tuning made general text worse and an 8% plain-text replay fixed it. The pico's replay sources (Wikipedia, Simple Wikipedia, SODA, FineMath, Orca-Math) stay in the 560M mix, and the fine-tune's replay is drawn from the anneal mix, text the model already knows.

Short, lower-case, no-question-mark questions were right at best 22% (casual facts 15%). The mix adds real casual phrasing (WildChat user turns, Stack Exchange question titles, DCLM-Edu's forum and Q&A style) and keeps its original casing.
The redo was dry: half-length answers. The mix prefers full-length answers: Stack Exchange answers of 20+ words, no FLAN-style one-word task data, no copied SQuAD spans.

The model copies the length and topic of earlier replies. Pretraining chats favour long multi-turn sets (smol-magpie-ultra, UltraChat, WildChat multi-turn); the mixed topic-switching chats stay in the fine-tune.

Greetings never stopped because a turn's end was not marked. Every assistant turn in pretraining chats ends with an end-of-turn mark (a reserved piece in the 16k list, or the pico's 'User:' marking), in exactly the fine-tune's layout.

Held-out samples change when the sources change, so compare by change from each run's own start. 1 in 100 documents per source is held out by a fixed hash, with the same list for every 560M run. The pico's held-out documents are also excluded, so per-letter wrongness compares fairly between the two models.
Try each new data step on a few hundred examples first. Every format, filter and decontamination rule runs on ~500 documents per source with samples read before the full CPU run.
Identity is tested ('Are you ChatGPT?', 'Who made you?'). Chats where the assistant names itself as another AI or company are removed, so pretraining does not teach a wrong name.
Facts are the weakest area and need varied wordings. Wikipedia stays at ~7% with Simple Wikipedia read 3-4 times, plus Nemotron's Q&A restatements and multi-answer Stack Exchange threads.
The word-piece list is built from a sample of the new mix with code included (decided 16 Nov). The tokenizer sample upweights code and maths, splits digits, and keeps indentation runs.

Data preparation would leave the GPUs idle for 30-60 minutes, and only one GPU job runs at a time. So all preparation runs on a separate cheap CPU machine as written scripts, and only finished piece files go to the GPU server.

finetune.summary_plain: When the 560M finishes reading its 80 billion pieces it knows a lot, but it cannot chat yet. This plan teaches it to chat with the recipe that fixed the 97M: practice chats that change topic and mark where each reply ends, reading practice that uses only questions the paragraph can answer, sums, who it is, and about a quarter plain text so it does not forget. Five things are new for the 560M: questions about code and computers, maths with the working shown, stories and poems, following instructions such as "in one sentence", and reading long texts or several search results at once. Before it learns to say "I don't know", we quiz the 560M itself to find out what it knows. The "knows" side gets every kind of question (short facts, sums, how and why), so it cannot learn "short question means I don't know" the way the 97M did. We train two versions from the same untouched starting model, one without and one with "I don't know" practice. We keep copies halfway, three-quarters of the way and at the end, then run every old test plus new ones: code, finding a hidden sentence in a 16,384-piece text, open requests with the chat page's settings, casual typing, questions late in a chat, and checks that "I don't know" has not spread. A last step that shows it a better and a worse answer (DPO) is optional. On a 1B model it lifted instruction-following a lot (IFEval 50.5 to 67.1) but added no facts. Almost all the practice data can be built and checked on the laptop before renting. Only the quiz and the training itself need the trained 560M, about 2 to 2.5 hours of server time (roughly $50-60 at $3 per GPU-hour). You approve the behaviour rules before anything is trained, and you choose which copy goes live.

behaviour_rules.rule: Lookup rule 1: if the paragraph (or one of several search results) has the answer, answer from it in full, natural sentences. Quoting it is fine.
behaviour_rules.why: The owner's rule. The 97M answered only with a few copied words, or said "The text doesn't say." when the paragraph did have the answer.
behaviour_rules.lesson: Owner decision (16 Nov lookup rules); SQuAD narrow answers

behaviour_rules.rule: Lookup rule 2: if no paragraph is useful (none was given, the search picked the wrong article, or the right article lacks this fact) and it knows the answer, it answers from memory as if lookup were off. It never says "The text doesn't say."
behaviour_rules.why: Lookup must never make an answer worse than lookup off.
behaviour_rules.lesson: Owner decision; answerable-only reading (doesn't-say leak, 165 of 1,300)

behaviour_rules.rule: Lookup rule 3: if no paragraph is useful and it does not know, it says "I don't know." The owner chooses the exact words, for example whether to add "You could try Look it up."
behaviour_rules.why: The owner's rule. Without practice the 97M made up 94 of 100 answers to impossible questions.
behaviour_rules.lesson: Owner decision; quiz the model itself

behaviour_rules.rule: Lookup on must never give a worse answer than lookup off for the same question. A question it gets right with lookup off must not turn into a wrong answer or "I don't know" with lookup on.
behaviour_rules.why: The owner's stated bar ("LOOKUP SHOULD NOT MAKE AN ANSWER WORSE"). It gets its own test.

behaviour_rules.rule: Questions with no real answer ("Who is the president of the Moon?", "Who won the 1850 FIFA World Cup?") are declined, not answered with something made up. DRAFT, for the owner to choose: either plain "I don't know.", or one short sentence saying the thing does not exist ("The Moon has no president."). The second option adds no other facts.
behaviour_rules.why: Making things up is the owner's main concern. Which wording to use is a behaviour choice, so the owner makes it.
behaviour_rules.lesson: IDK spread by question shape (no-real-answer questions); owner decides behaviour

behaviour_rules.rule: "I don't know" is only for fact questions it cannot answer. It is never the reply to sums or word problems, requests to write, explain or fix code, stories, poems, jokes, advice, opinions, explanations of everyday things, greetings, or questions about itself.
behaviour_rules.why: On the 97M redo, "Tell me a short story" and 19 of 50 sums got "I don't know."
behaviour_rules.lesson: IDK spread by question shape; dry replies

behaviour_rules.rule: The length of a reply fits the request. "capital of france?" gets one sentence, perhaps with one extra detail. "What is photosynthesis?" gets a short paragraph of 3-5 sentences. "Tell me about X", "Explain X" and long requests get several paragraphs (about 100-300 words). Explicit instructions ("in one sentence", "list three") are followed exactly.
behaviour_rules.why: The owner found the redo dry (117 words against 218 before). A phrasing like "Tell me about" must not be tied to short answers.

behaviour_rules.rule: A casual question (lower-case, no question mark, cut short: "capital of canada", "15+27=") is answered exactly like its formal version.
behaviour_rules.why: Casual questions were right half as often as formal ones on the 97M (15% against 32%), and "capital of france?" was right only about half the time.

behaviour_rules.rule: Every reply stops at the end of its own turn. It never writes the user's next line. A greeting gets a short, friendly reply.
behaviour_rules.why: Before the turn ends were marked, the 97M kept writing after "Hello! How can I help you today?" (only 49 of 60 greetings ended properly).

behaviour_rules.rule: In a long chat, a new question is answered on its own topic. The topic, length or mistakes of earlier replies do not carry into it: after short replies it still gives a full answer when asked, and an earlier wrong reply is not repeated or built on.
behaviour_rules.why: The model copies the length and topic of earlier replies (study tips shrank to about 22 words, 22 of 30 about plants). After a wrong sodium answer, "capital of france?" was right 0 of 20 times.
behaviour_rules.lesson: First reply sets the style; wrong answer drags the next ones down

behaviour_rules.rule: Identity: it is SlingerGPT, made by Ishtdeep, also known as Gunslinger. It is not ChatGPT, Claude or any other assistant, and it is an AI, not a person. The owner writes the new wording for its size and history (the 97M's answers say "about 97 million weights" and "trained on a single laptop", which will be untrue).
behaviour_rules.why: The owner decides the identity wording.

behaviour_rules.rule: Code (DRAFT): when asked to write code, it gives complete code in a fenced block with a short plain explanation, in Python unless another language is named. When asked to fix code, it says in one or two sentences what was wrong, then gives the corrected code. When asked to explain code, it explains step by step in plain words.
behaviour_rules.why: New skill. The default language and the layout are the owner's choice.

behaviour_rules.rule: Maths (DRAFT): word problems show short working steps and end with "The answer is N." A bare sum gets a one-line worked answer ("15 + 27 = 42.").
behaviour_rules.why: This keeps the 97M's maths layout, which took sums from 72% to 94%.

behaviour_rules.rule: Creative requests (story, poem, joke, song idea) are always attempted at full length. They are never declined, as long as they are harmless.
behaviour_rules.why: The owner's own "Tell me a short story" got "I don't know." on the 97M redo.

behaviour_rules.rule: Long texts and several results: with a long document or many search results, it answers from whichever part holds the answer, wherever that part sits. Rules 1-3 apply as for one paragraph.

Search by itself (OPTIONAL, only if the owner wants it): when search is on and it does not know, it writes one search line instead of guessing. When it knows, it answers directly with no search. After the results arrive, rules 1-3 apply.
behaviour_rules.why: The owner asked whether it should run the search itself. This adds a step to the chat page.

behaviour_rules.rule: Harmful requests (DRAFT, owner decides whether this is included at all): a short, polite decline with no lecture. The 97M had no such practice.
behaviour_rules.why: This is a behaviour choice, and it can make the model decline harmless look-alike requests. That would be checked with CoCoNot's contrast set.

stages.name: 0. Quiz the base 560M (what does it know?)
stages.what: The finished base model (after the 16,384 phase) is quizzed on about 120,000 questions with checked answers in six shapes. For each one we measure how likely it finds the real answer, lookup off (answer_wrongness, the method that worked on the 97M). For short-answer questions we also sample 10 answers with the page's settings and match them against the answer list. This picks the questions it knows (used for rule-2 practice, the 'knows' side and search practice) and the ones it does not (the 'I don't know' side). The cut-offs are re-set for the 560M on 500 checkable items (the 97M used at most 0.5 = knows and at least 0.75 = does not, with the middle left out). Then 30 items from each side go to the owner to read before any training.
stages.pieces: About 40M pieces read and about 12M written (forward passes only, nothing learned)
stages.time_8xB200: about 10-20 minutes, plus building the knows/search data on the CPU (a few minutes)

stages.name: 1. Learning-rate check
stages.what: Three short fine-tunes from the base with the full mix, at 1/10, 1/5 and 1/3 of the main run's peak learning rate (the 97M's fine-tune used 1/5: 0.0004 against 0.002). Each is scored on held-out chats, reading, maths and general text, judged by the change from its own start. Recipes such as SmolLM2's 3e-4 or 1e-3 and Tulu's 5e-6 were tuned for AdamW and do not carry over to Muon, so the rate has to be found again.
stages.learning_rate: 1/10, 1/5 and 1/3 of the main run's peak, 30 steps warm-up, cosine down

stages.name: 2A. Main fine-tune, candidate A (rules 1-2, no 'I don't know' practice)
stages.what: Fresh from the base model with a fresh optimiser, using the full mix in the data list without line 12 (its 3% goes to the chat line). This is the safe version, the same idea as the 97M's accepted chat2: chats, mixed chats, code and CS, maths, instructions, creative, answerable reading, several results, long-window practice, identity, 23% plain and general text. Only Assistant pieces, turn-end 'User:' names and the final end-of-text are practised (the 97M's marks). Copies are kept at steps 1,200, 1,800 and 2,400. Scale against the 97M: 2,000 to 2,400 steps, but each step is 8 times bigger (524,288 pieces against 65,536), so it reads 9.6 times the pieces (1.26B against 131M). That is about 2.6 pieces per weight against 1.35. Measured against pretraining it is 1.6% against the 97M's 2.2%. The extra is for 13 sources where the 97M had 7. Each source should be read at most about 2 times (Tulu 3 and SmolLM2 stopped at 2 passes); fix the steps once the pieces are counted.
stages.learning_rate: The peak picked in stage 1 (expected about 1/5 of the main run's peak), 100 steps warm-up, cosine down to 10%, gradient clipping 1.0, Muon as in the main run
stages.window: 16,384 (the model's own window, as the 97M used its own 2,048). Short chats sit several to a window, as before. Long practice items are placed whole, never cut.
stages.time_8xB200: about 15-25 minutes (at roughly 1.2-2M pieces a second; the main run's measured speed replaces this)

stages.name: 2B. Main fine-tune, candidate B (A + 'I don't know' practice, rule 3)
stages.what: Exactly as 2A, also from the base and never on top of A, with line 12 (knows or not, 3%) added. Both candidates are tested, so the owner can see what rule-3 practice costs and gains. If the spread checks fail, the fix is diagnosed by question shape and the data rebalanced, then B is redone from the base (fix before reject).

stages.name: 3. Preference step (DPO)
stages.what: Starts from the SFT copy the owner picks and is tested against it as a separate candidate. It is never used to patch data problems: those go into a redo of stage 2. Pairs: UltraFeedback binarized (61.1k, the set SmolLM2 found most consistently helpful and used for 135M, 360M and 1.7B). Optional project pairs: chosen = the checked answer, rejected = the 560M's own made-up answer to a question it does not know, and the same the other way round for known questions where it wrongly said "I don't know." finetune.knows_method:
How the 560M learns rule 3 ("I don't know") without it spreading:
1. Before renting, build the question pool on the laptop: about 120,000 questions with checked answers, in six shapes.
   (a) "What is X?" / "Who was X?", answered with a FineWiki opening of 2-4 sentences.
   (b) "Tell me about X" / "Explain X", answered with the whole lead paragraph (about 80-250 words).
   (c) Short narrow facts: TriviaQA no-context and NQ short-answer questions. The answer is the evidence or long-answer sentence that holds the short answer (checked text, a full sentence).
   (d) How and why questions from NQ, answered with the long-answer paragraph.
   (e) Casual retypings of all of the above, using casual().
   (f) No-real-answer questions built as twins of real questions in the same shapes: "Who won the 1998 FIFA World Cup?" is real, "Who won the 1850 FIFA World Cup?" is not. Same for "Who is the president of France?" and "Who is the president of the Moon?". A small CoCoNot slice is added.
   Sums, word problems, code, stories and advice are never quizzed: they always stay on the "answers" side. Every item whose words overlap the tests is removed (test_words, and the 2-content-word rule that no_answer() uses).
2. Stage 0 on the server quizzes the finished base 560M, with lookup off and in the chat page's layout. The measure is how likely it finds the real answer (answer_wrongness, wrongness per letter). This is the method that worked on the 97M; quizzing SQuAD without paragraphs and judging its own answers by shared words were both dropped. On short-answer shapes it also samples 10 answers with the page's settings and matches them against TriviaQA/NQ answer aliases. An item counts as known only if both measures agree; disagreements are dropped. Its own answers are only measured, never used for training.
3. Set the cut-offs for the 560M rather than copying the 97M's 0.5/0.75. On 500 checkable short-answer items, choose them so the "knows" side is right at least 85% of the time and the "does not know" side at most 10%. The unsure middle is left out. Show the owner 30 random items from each side before training, as with the 97M's look= printout.
4. Balance by shape (the 97M's failure was that every "knows" example was "What is X?" while half the "I don't know" examples were short SQuAD questions). Every shape (a)-(f) gets the same fraction of "I don't know", lengths are matched, and there are as many "knows" as "does not know" overall. Known items are answered with the checked reference at full natural length. The block also holds sums (10% of it), code and open requests, never with "I don't know", so the model cannot learn "short question means I don't know" or "Tell me... means I don't know".
5. Each item comes with no paragraph (lookup off) or, half the time, a useless paragraph: another article, or the real lookup.py's wrong pick for that question. Known gets the memory answer (rule 2); unknown gets "I don't know." (rule 3). Rule 1 (the paragraph has it) is taught by the reading lines, which also include questions the model does not know, so it does not learn "I don't know whenever I don't know, even if the paragraph says".
6. Only candidate B gets this block (3%). Candidate A is the control. Afterwards the spread checks run: sums, narrow facts it knew, open requests, the CoCoNot contrast set, and a per-shape table. If a check fails, find which shape it spread to, rebalance that shape, and redo B from the base (fix before reject; never a top-up).
finetune.chats_design:
Layout: keep the layout that works ("System: ...", "User: ...", "Assistant: ..." lines, with an end-of-text piece after a chat). The same layout must be used for the ~3-5% of conversation data in pretraining, so the fine-tune starts from a model that already knows it. Optionally reserve one spare "end of turn" piece in the 16,384 list now: it costs nothing, and it is only possible before the tokenizer is built.

What is practised: only Assistant pieces; the "User:" name after a practised reply (turn_ends, which fixed greetings that never stopped); the final end-of-text. System and user text are read but never practised.

Chat shapes: chats are 1 to about 16,000 pieces long (the 97M's went to about 2,000), so late turns of long chats are practised. Several unrelated topics sit in one chat with no end-of-text between them. Short replies (greetings, "thanks", bare sums, one-sentence requests) are mixed with long ones (explanations, stories, code), and a long answer often follows short replies. Follow-ups stay on topic ("explain more", "why was he killed?"). In 10% of chats an earlier reply is wrong (another chat's answer): it is read, never practised, so the next answer stays good. 30% of user turns are typed casually (lower-case, no question mark, "capital of canada"). The System line is there 60% of the time. Openings are varied: everyday-conversations always opens with "Hello! How can I help you today?", so vary it.

New kinds of turns: code requests (write, explain, fix) with fenced code; computer-basics questions; maths with working; creative requests; long documents and several results in the System line, in the exact format the chat page will send; optionally a "Search:" turn. Who-are-you questions appear fresh and late in long chats.

Real-user prompts (WildChat, oasst2) supply natural, short and messy phrasing. No public set targets topic switching, so the mixed builder does that job.

Page settings: test with the page's settings (temperature 0.3, top-k 50, anti-repetition 0.8, 300 words). Two settings may need to change for code. The 300-word cap cuts long code. The anti-repetition setting may garble code, which legitimately repeats names and indentation: test with it on and off, and if needed let it skip code blocks the way dry_from skips the passage. Both are the owner's choice.
finetune.lookup_practice:
The owner's three rules are taught as separate, matched pieces:

Rule 1 (the paragraph has it): single-passage reading uses answerable questions only. That means SQuAD 2.0's answerable part, NQ (lower-case, search-style questions, the phrasing the project lacked), CoQA's Wikipedia and literature parts, and QuAC without its CANNOTANSWER turns. Answers are full sentences: the passage sentence that holds the answer, so the answer is real checked text and not a few copied words. Broad questions ("What is photosynthesis?") get the opening paragraph at full length, never one sentence. 25% are typed casually. The passage goes in the System line exactly as the page sends it ("Answer using this passage from Wikipedia (title): ..."). Part of the passages come from the real lookup.py search, including its wrong picks, so practice matches what the page really sends.

Several results: HotpotQA distractor (10 paragraphs, 2 relevant), TriviaQA rc (about 6 documents), Glaive RAG grounded and mixed. Results are shuffled so the answer can be in any position; every example's answer is in at least one result (checked by string match). The several-results format on the page must be fixed first, and practice must use exactly it.

Rule 2 (useless paragraph, it knows): questions the stage-0 quiz says the 560M knows, given another article's paragraph or the search's wrong pick, are answered from memory with the checked reference answer. This is in both candidates. It never says "The text doesn't say."

Rule 3 (useless paragraph, does not know): "I don't know.", from the quiz, in candidate B only (see knows_method). SQuAD's no-answer questions are not used at all: with a paragraph they caused the doesn't-say leak, and without one they caused the spread by question shape.

Never worse: the lookup-on-against-off test checks every question both ways.

Writing replies: the anti-repetition check must skip every passage and result (dry_from covers the System line), or quoting gets garbled.

Search by itself (optional): the model writes "Search: <key words>" (the words are built by code, never the model's own), the page runs lookup.py, the results arrive in the System/results format, and rules 1-3 apply. It is practised only on questions the quiz says it does not know; known questions are answered directly.
finetune.against_forgetting:
1. Plain text in the mix: 15% general text (FineWeb-Edu top pages, Cosmopedia, top Stack-Edu code) plus 8% plain pre-training text (FineWiki en and simple, SODA, FineMath-4+, Orca-Math, and some long books and papers at 16k), every piece practised. The 97M's 8% plain text brought held-out text back from 0.5424 to 0.5382, and its 20% general text kept what it knew. Code and long text are added because the 560M's coding and 16k skill come from pretraining.
2. A gentle, short run: the peak learning rate is about 1/5 of the main run's (checked in stage 1); 1.26B pieces is about 1.6% of the 80B pretraining (the 97M: 2.2%); each fine-tune source is read at most about 2 times.
3. Copies kept partway (1,200, 1,800 and 2,400 of 2,400): on the 97M, general-text error peaked about a quarter of the way in and then fell, and maths was best at 75%.
4. Redo from the base, never top up: every candidate (A, B, and any fix) starts from the same pretrained base with a fresh optimiser. A 600-step top-up on the 97M made the quiz and the sums worse. The optional preference step is a separate candidate, tested against its parent, and never used to patch data problems.
5. Measure forgetting against the model's own start: held-out wrongness per letter of the fine-tuned copy against the base, judged by the full test, not the training log's small samples (they jump by about 0.01). The needle test is run on the base and after the fine-tune, so long-window skill is checked too.
6. If preference tuning hurts the long window (SmolLM3 saw this with APO), merge with the SFT parent (stage 4).
finetune.copies_and_settings:
Starting point: the finished base 560M after the 16,384 phase (about 492M weights with the 4x Engram). Every candidate starts from it with a fresh optimiser; no candidate starts from another.
Optimiser and maths: Muon as in the main run; 8-bit training maths as in the main run, with the same choice of layers that stay 16-bit. If the page will write in 8-bit, use scales that do not depend on other tokens (per token or per row), as the 97M lesson says.
Batch: 32 windows of 16,384 = 524,288 pieces a step (4 windows per GPU; if memory is short, 2 windows with 2 accumulations). The 97M's step was 65,536 pieces in windows of 2,048.
Length: 2,400 steps (about 1.26B pieces). Change this once the pieces are counted, so that no source is read more than about 2 times.
Learning rate: the peak from the stage-1 check (expected about 1/5 of the main run's peak, the 97M's 0.0004 against 0.002), 100 steps warm-up, cosine down to 10%, gradient clipping 1.0.
Marks: Assistant pieces, the turn-end "User:" name, and the final end-of-text. General and plain text: every piece.
Copies: <name>_A_1200, _A_1800, _A_2400 and <name>_B_1200, _B_1800, _B_2400 under models/candidates/, each with its tokenizer file (as keep() does now). A candidate stays off the chat page's picker. When files are moved, update the scripts that load them by name (lesson).
Log: held-out scores per source every 100 steps (chats, mixed, reading, several results, long, code, maths, knows, general, plain). Compare runs by the change from their own start.
Before the full run: a few hundred examples of every new builder are read by eye, and a 2-step run checks that marks line up with replies (the 97M caught answers shifted by a few letters this way).
Optional preference step: from the copy the owner picks, about 1,270 steps of 128 pairs, LR from a 3-point sweep (SmolLM2: 1e-6 AdamW, beta 0.5, 2 passes, length 1,024).

tests.test: chat_suite.py run + compare (the page's code and settings, 10 tries per item)
tests.checks: 1,300 replies: facts formal and casual, casual sums, topic switch, after a wrong answer, follow-ups, length in a new chat and after 'Hello!', greetings ending, identity fresh and late, instructions, facts late in a chat, impossible questions, cut-offs and repeated phrases
tests.pass_rule: No measure WORSE (z <= -2) against the 97M live model (slingergpt1_pico_chat2), and the 560M copies compared with each other. 'The text doesn't say.' stays at 0. Repetition is judged among 150+ word replies only (97M chat2: 74%), not overall. Needs chat_server support for the 560M (KV cache at 16k) and the new identity wording in WHO.

tests.test: test_slinger.py run (held-out text, 117-question quiz, 12 chat questions)
tests.checks: Wrongness per letter on held-out documents of the 560M's own mix; quiz picking and own words; greedy and sampled answers
tests.pass_rule: Held-out wrongness rises at most 0.006 per letter over the 560M base (97M accepted run: +0.004, 0.5319 -> 0.5360). Quiz picking and own words not below the base's. Needs the 560M's held-out files and config; judged on the full test, not the training log.

tests.test: test_slinger.py extra (sums, identity, lookup, broad, no-real-answer, quiz with passage)
tests.checks: 50 sums; 20 identity questions fresh and after a long answer; 30 narrow lookup questions and 30 broad ones, with and without the passage; 10 no-real-answer questions; the quiz with its passage
tests.pass_rule: Sums >= 48/50; identity 20/20 (new wording); broad with lookup right >= 28/30 and 'not said' 0; quiz with passage picking not below the base's; no-real-answer declined: candidate B >= 8/10 (candidate A reported only).

tests.checks: Every measure of test_slinger run and extra against a baseline
tests.pass_rule: Reports ADOPT or KEEP against the 97M chat2 and between the 560M copies. It only reports; the owner decides which copy is kept.

tests.checks: The 60 lookup and broad questions, the 117 quiz items and 60 new casual fact questions, each asked with lookup off and on, 5 tries each with the page's settings. Counts the questions where lookup on turns a right answer into a wrong one or 'I don't know'.
tests.pass_rule: Zero questions right with lookup off (>= 4 of 5) that turn wrong or 'I don't know' with lookup on (<= 1 of 5), and right-with-lookup >= right-without in every group. This is the owner's rule.

tests.checks: HumanEval (164) and MBPP pass@1, greedy, run in a sandbox (both kept out of practice data); 30 built fix-the-bug items checked by unit tests; 30 explain-this-code items with keyword checks; 60 computer-basics questions (RAM, CPU, files and folders, ls/cd, IP address, https, viruses, shortcuts) formal and casual, 10 tries with the page's settings; code requests run with anti-repetition on and off and with 300 and 600 words
tests.pass_rule: Code pass@1 above the 560M base's few-shot score on the same problems; fix-the-bug >= 50%; computer basics right >= 85% formal and >= 75% casual; 0 'I don't know' replies to code requests; anti-repetition setting does not lower pass@1 (else the owner decides the page setting).

tests.test: Long-window needle and wrongness by position (new)
tests.checks: A fact sentence put at 10 depths in held-out PG-19 test books cut to 2k, 4k, 8k, 12k and 16k pieces, asked in chat layout; wrongness by position on 100 held-out PG-19 test books
tests.pass_rule: Found >= 90% at every depth up to 16,384, and not below the base model's score (asked as plain continuation) before the fine-tune; wrongness does not rise after position 4,096.

tests.test: Find the detail and several results (new)
tests.checks: 100 held-out long documents (Qasper and NarrativeQA test windows, long FineWiki articles) with questions; 100 HotpotQA validation questions with 10 results and 50 with about 30 results (about 8k pieces)
tests.pass_rule: Right with 30 results within 10 points of right with 10 results; 0 'I don't know' when the answer is in the text; right not below the single-passage reading rate minus 15 points.

tests.test: Open requests with the page's settings (new)
tests.checks: 20 open requests (short story, poem, joke, advice, study tips, 'Explain how a computer works', 'The capital of France is?', 'What is photosynthesis?', 'Tell me about the solar system'), 10 tries each at temperature 0.3, top-k 50, anti-repetition 0.8, 300 words
tests.pass_rule: 0 'I don't know' replies; long requests median >= 150 words (97M first fine-tune 218, the redo the owner found dry 117); 'What is photosynthesis?' 3+ sentences in >= 8 of 10; the owner reads 20 replies before accepting.

tests.checks: 100 facts asked formally and casually (lower-case, no question mark, cut short), including the owner's 'capital of france?' 100 times in a fresh chat
tests.pass_rule: Casual right >= 90% of formal right; 'capital of france?' right >= 90 of 100.

tests.checks: 30 long chats (2k-12k pieces, several topics, short and long replies mixed, some with a wrong answer in them), each ending in a new fact question or a long-answer request
tests.pass_rule: Right >= 90% of the fresh-chat rate; old topic or wrong answer leaks in <= 10%; long-answer length after short replies >= 70% of the fresh-chat length.

tests.test: 'I don't know' spread checks (new; after any rule-3 practice)
tests.checks: 50 sums + 30 bare sums; 200 held-out narrow facts the base quiz scored as known; the CoCoNot contrast set (379 harmless look-alikes); the 20 open requests; a per-shape table of 'I don't know' on known held-out questions (What is / Tell me about / short / casual / how-why); 20 new no-real-answer questions x 10 tries; 200 held-out questions the quiz scored as unknown
tests.pass_rule: 0 'I don't know' on sums and open requests; known narrow facts still right >= 95% of candidate A's rate; CoCoNot contrast answered >= 90%; 'I don't know' on known questions <= 5% in every shape; no-real-answer declined >= 80 of 100; unknown questions: declined share reported for the owner's trade-off (no fixed bar).

tests.checks: GSM8K test (1,319, greedy, kept out of practice data); IFEval (541 prompts, kept out); chat_suite's instruction items
tests.pass_rule: GSM8K above the base 5-shot; chat_suite instructions >= 70% (97M chat2). Published reference points, not bars: SmolLM2-360M-Instruct IFEval 41.0, GSM8K 7.43 (5-shot); Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct 31.6, 26.8.

tests.checks: 'capital of france?' x 100 and the 30 casual facts x 10, written in 16-bit and in 8-bit
tests.pass_rule: 8-bit within chance (z < 2) of 16-bit before the page writes in 8-bit.

finetune.prepare_beforehand:
On the laptop, before renting (no trained 560M needed):
1. The owner approves the behaviour rules and the chat and results formats. The decision on a spare end-of-turn piece must come before the 16,384 tokenizer is built.
2. List every fine-tune dataset with its size and licence for the owner's OK, then download them. NQ's full 45 GB and WildChat are better downloaded on the server or replaced by smaller copies, which is also the owner's call.
3. Extend the builders in finetune_slinger.py: mixed (longer, with code and long-answer turns); reading (full-sentence answers, NQ/CoQA/QuAC); broad (whole lead paragraph); several results; long practice (whole items placed unbroken in 16k windows); code and CS (Stack Exchange formatting, tldr, fix-the-bug with test runs); maths; instruction; creative; identity for the 560M; search practice (all but the quiz split). Extend test_words to every new test (HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K test, IFEval, CoCoNot contrast, the needle books and sentences, new chat and code questions), and add 13-word overlap removal for benchmarks.
4. Tokenize everything with the new 16k tokenizer, count the pieces per source, set the steps so no source is read more than about 2 times, and read a few hundred examples of every builder by eye.
5. Build the quiz pool (about 120,000 questions with checked answers, six shapes, false-premise twins) so it only needs scoring on the day.
6. Write the 8-GPU fine-tune (the same Windows/marks/copies code under DDP, plus whole-item placement) and rehearse the whole pipeline end to end on the 97M: a 200-step run with the new mix and a 2-step mark check (catches shifted answers). Also write the optional DPO script and test it on the 97M at tiny scale.
7. Write the new tests (lookup-never-worse, code sandbox, needle, find-the-detail, open requests, casual, late-in-chat, IDK spread, GSM8K/IFEval, 8-bit against 16-bit) and run them on the 97M chat2 now. That debugs them and gives the baseline.
8. chat_server support for the 560M: KV cache, compile and CUDA graphs up to 16,384, and the several-results format with anti-repetition skipping them.
One GPU job at a time on the laptop: chat server off while testing; helper scripts written to files.

Needs the trained 560M (on the server, same day):
- Stage 0 quiz and the cut-offs (rule-2, knows and search splits).
- The learning-rate check.
- The base model's own scores (held-out, needle as plain continuation, code few-shot, GSM8K 5-shot) as the 'own start'.
- Preference pairs that use the 560M's own wrong answers as 'rejected' (optional).
- The A and B runs and their tests.
owner_decisions: Approve or change each behaviour rule (lookup rules 1-3 are already yours; the drafts on answer length, code, maths, creative, identity and harmful requests are not decided).
No-real-answer questions: plain "I don't know." or one short sentence saying it does not exist ("The Moon has no president.")?
"I don't know" practice: train both candidate A (without) and B (with) and choose after the tests, as proposed, or only one?
The new identity wording: name (SlingerGPT 1 ... ?), size (about 492 million weights), and how it was trained (a rented server, not a single laptop).

Chat layout: keep the working "System:/User:/Assistant:" lines, and whether to reserve one spare end-of-turn piece in the 16,384 list. This must be decided before the tokenizer is built, before pretraining.
The layout the chat page uses for several search results, and the System line text for the 560M.

Licences: will the model ever be used commercially? That decides whether to skip non-commercial sets (No Robots, LongAlpaca, ChatQA2, parts of the Tulu/OLMo preference mixes) and whether to accept sets with no stated licence (OpenHermes 2.5, Magpie-Ultra v1.0, LongAlign-10k, the QuALITY mirror, TriviaQA 'unknown'), Reddit text (WritingPrompts), model-output terms (OpenAI, Llama 3.1, Qwen), gated sets (xLAM) and the Stack Exchange copy.
Preference step (DPO): try it or not. If yes: only the ready-made UltraFeedback pairs, or also pairs where the 560M's own made-up answers are the 'worse' side?
May the 560M's own answers that were checked (a sum that computes right, code that passes tests) ever count as 'good' examples? Default: no, reference answers only.
Should it learn to run the search itself (optional search practice, and a change to the chat page)?
Include any harmful-request declines, or none as on the 97M?
Jokes: no joke dataset with a confirmed licence was found. Skip jokes, or write a small set by hand?
Default code language (Python proposed), and the page's 300-word limit and anti-repetition setting for code replies.
Write replies in 8-bit or 16-bit on the page (8-bit answered unsure questions worse on the 97M).
Keep the server rented through the tests (about 1 more hour, so a fix-and-redo can run at once) or copy the base home and re-rent later?
Which copy goes live, after reading the test results and replies.
